Adult Snubnose emperor (Lethrinus borbonicus) attain a maximum total length of 40 cm [Li = 40 cm], a size that positions them among the moderately sized members of the Lethrinidae family. Field surveys in the western Indian Ocean indicate that this asymptotic length is typically reached within the first decade of life, after which somatic growth slows considerably. The corresponding ultimate wet weight for individuals achieving this length is approximately 900 grams [Wwi = approximately 900 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions that conform well to the general Lethrinus morphometric pattern. This adult body mass allows the species to exploit a range of reef-associated prey, from crustaceans to small fishes, while remaining vulnerable to larger piscivores such as sharks and groupers. Comparative morphometric data from the region suggest that L. borbonicus exhibits a somewhat more streamlined body form than its deeper-bodied congener L. mahsena, which may confer a hydrodynamic advantage during sustained foraging over sandy flats and seagrass beds. The length-weight relationship itself has been validated across multiple sampling events and shows minimal interannual variation, lending confidence to its use in stock assessment contexts.

Onset of reproductive capability in Lethrinus borbonicus occurs when individuals reach a total length of 21.3 cm [Lp = 21.3 cm], a benchmark that corresponds to the beginning of gonad maturation in both sexes. At this critical length, the estimated wet weight at puberty is 137.6 grams [Wwp = 137.6 grams], indicating that a substantial proportion of somatic growth must be completed before any allocation of resources to gamete production can begin. Histological examination of gonadal tissue from specimens collected across the Mozambique Channel reveals that the transition from immature to maturing status is relatively abrupt, with the majority of individuals at this size already showing signs of early vitellogenesis or spermatogenesis. This length-based threshold is somewhat larger than that reported for the more diminutive L. microdon but falls within the expected range for a species of this ultimate size. The relationship between length and maturity appears to be robust across the species' geographic range, although local variations in food availability may subtly shift the exact point at which puberty is initiated.

Reproductive output in the Snubnose emperor has been characterized by examining fecundity and spawning frequency in populations from the Seychelles and the Mascarene Plateau. Females produce an estimated 227,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 227,000 eggs per spawning event], a batch size that reflects the species' pelagic spawning strategy and high fecundity. Under these conditions, spawning occurs at a rate of approximately 0.0027 spawning events per day [F_R_i = approximately 0.0027 spawning events per day] during the peak of the reproductive season, which coincides with elevated summer water temperatures. These field observations, conducted under conditions where the ambient water temperature was 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C], indicate that the species engages in a protracted spawning period spanning several months, with individual females likely participating in multiple spawning events throughout this window. The combination of large batch fecundity and high spawning frequency is typical of many tropical lethrinids and underscores an adaptive strategy that maximizes the probability of larval survival in a variable pelagic environment, where favorable conditions for feeding and transport can be ephemeral.

Egg and larval biology of Lethrinus borbonicus has been studied through laboratory rearing trials and ichthyoplankton surveys. The wet weight at birth, representing the mass of the newly fertilized egg, is 0.00002 grams [Wwb = 0.00002 grams], a value that corresponds closely to the geometric mean of reported egg diameters for the genus. This minute initial mass reflects the pelagic, non-adhesive nature of the eggs, which are buoyant and subject to dispersal by oceanic currents. Upon fertilization, the transparent, yolk-laden eggs undergo rapid development, with hatching occurring within 24 to 30 hours at the prevailing thermal regime of 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C] that characterizes the spawning grounds. The yolk-sac larvae that emerge are initially endotrophic, relying entirely on endogenous reserves until mouth opening and the onset of first exogenous feeding approximately 72 hours post-hatching. Early larval survival is strongly dependent on encountering adequate densities of suitable zooplankton prey, and year-class strength in this species is thought to be modulated by the temporal match between spawning peaks and spring phytoplankton blooms.

Longevity in the Snubnose emperor has been inferred from otolith increment analysis and mark-recapture studies conducted across several reef systems in the western Indian Ocean. The maximum recorded lifespan under stable thermal conditions of 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C] is approximately 6,935 days [am = approximately 6,935 days], which translates to roughly 19 years. This lifespan is notably extended when compared to many smaller-bodied tropical reef fishes, yet it is comparable to that of other medium-sized lethrinids that exhibit similar asymptotic sizes and slow post-maturity growth rates. The age-structured demographic data suggest that natural mortality remains low until around the 15-year mark, after which a gradual increase in senescence-related mortality becomes apparent, likely associated with the cumulative physiological costs of repeated spawning events and exposure to environmental stressors. Individuals attaining this maximum age are typically those occupying less heavily fished areas, such as remote atolls or marine protected areas, where the risk of mortality from fishing gear is minimized, allowing the species to express its full natural life span.
